section.title: Oracles against Ammon, Edom, and the East
section.sectionRationale: This chapter gathers five shorter oracles: Ammon, who had seized Israelite land; Edom, Israel's brother nation through Esau; Damascus, the old Aramean capital; Kedar and Hazor, the tent dwelling peoples of the eastern desert; and Elam, far to the east near Persia. Each nation is judged for its own particular pride or violence, and three of the five close with an unlooked-for promise of restoration.
section.thesis: The LORD's justice reaches every neighbor of Judah, near or far, kin or stranger, tent dweller or walled city; and even here His severity is threaded through with promises that He will one day restore what He has broken.
section.frameNote: Five movements, one nation each: Ammon, who seized Gad's land; Edom, proud in the clefts of the rocks; Damascus, agitated like the sea; Kedar and Hazor, a people dwelling alone; and Elam, whose bow will be shattered yet whose captivity will be turned in the last days.

verses.text: Concerning the Ammonites, this is what the LORD says: “Has Israel no sons? Is he without heir? Why then has {{milcom|Milcom}} taken possession of Gad? Why have his people settled in their cities?

Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will sound the battle cry against Rabbah of the Ammonites. It will become a heap of ruins, and its villages will be burned. Then Israel will drive out their dispossessors, says the LORD.

Wail, O Heshbon, for Ai has been destroyed; cry out, O daughters of Rabbah! Put on sackcloth and mourn; run back and forth within your walls, for Milcom will go into exile together with his priests and officials.
Why do you boast of your valleys, your valleys so fruitful, O faithless daughter? You trust in your riches and say, ‘Who can come against me?’
Behold, I am about to bring terror upon you, declares the Lord GOD of Hosts, from all those around you. You will each be driven headlong, with no one to regather the fugitives.
Yet afterward I will {{shuvshevut|restore}} the Ammonites from captivity,” declares the LORD.

units.label: Concerning Edom
units.note: wisdom failed, pride in the rocks answered

verses.text: Concerning Edom, this is what the LORD of Hosts says: “Is there no longer wisdom in Teman? Has counsel perished from the prudent? Has their wisdom decayed?
Turn and run! Lie low, O dwellers of Dedan, for I will bring disaster on Esau at the time I punish him.
If grape gatherers came to you, would they not leave some gleanings? Were thieves to come in the night, would they not steal only what they wanted?

But I will strip Esau bare; I will uncover his hiding places, and he will be unable to conceal himself. His descendants will be destroyed along with his relatives and neighbors, and he will be no more.
Abandon your orphans; I will preserve their lives. Let your widows trust in Me.”
For this is what the LORD says: “If those who do not deserve to drink the cup must drink it, can you possibly remain unpunished? You will not go unpunished, for you must drink it too.
For by Myself I have sworn, declares the LORD, that Bozrah will become a desolation, a disgrace, a ruin, and a curse, and all her cities will be in ruins forever.”
I have heard a message from the LORD; an envoy has been sent to the nations: “Assemble yourselves to march against her! Rise up for battle!”
“For behold, I will make you small among nations, despised among men.

The terror you cause and the pride of your heart have deceived you, O dwellers in the clefts of the rocks, O occupiers of the mountain summit. Though you elevate your nest like the eagle, even from there I will bring you down,” declares the LORD.
“Edom will become an object of horror. All who pass by will be appalled and will scoff at all her wounds.
As Sodom and Gomorrah were overthrown along with their neighbors,” says the LORD, “no one will dwell there; no man will abide there.

Behold, one will come up like a lion from the thickets of the Jordan to the watered pasture. For in an instant I will chase Edom from her land. Who is the chosen one I will appoint for this? For who is like Me, and who can challenge Me? What shepherd can stand against Me?”

Therefore hear the plans that the LORD has drawn up against Edom and the strategies He has devised against the people of Teman: Surely the little ones of the flock will be dragged away; certainly their pasture will be made desolate because of them.
At the sound of their fall the earth will quake; their cry will resound to the Red Sea.
Look! An eagle will soar and swoop down, spreading its wings over Bozrah. In that day the hearts of Edom’s mighty men will be like the heart of a woman in labor.
Concerning Damascus: “Hamath and Arpad are put to shame, for they have heard a bad report; they are agitated like the sea; their anxiety cannot be calmed.
Damascus has become feeble; she has turned to flee. Panic has gripped her; anguish and pain have seized her like a woman in labor.
How is the city of praise not forsaken, the town that brings Me joy?
For her young men will fall in the streets, and all her warriors will be silenced in that day,” declares the LORD of Hosts.
“I will set fire to the walls of Damascus; it will consume the fortresses of Ben-hadad.”

units.label: Concerning Kedar and Hazor
units.note: a people dwelling alone, without gates or bars

verses.text: Concerning Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor, which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon defeated, this is what the LORD says: “Rise up, advance against Kedar, and destroy the people of the east!
They will take their tents and flocks, their tent curtains and all their goods. They will take their camels for themselves. They will shout to them: ‘Terror is on every side!’
Run! Escape quickly! Lie low, O residents of Hazor,” declares the LORD, “for Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has drawn up a plan against you; he has devised a strategy against you.
Rise up, advance against a nation at ease, one that dwells securely,” declares the LORD. “They have no gates or bars; they live alone.

Their camels will become plunder, and their large herds will be spoil. I will scatter to the wind in every direction those who shave their temples; I will bring calamity on them from all sides,” declares the LORD.
“Hazor will become a haunt for jackals, a desolation forever. No one will dwell there; no man will abide there.”

units.label: Concerning Elam
units.note: the bow shattered, yet restored at last

verses.text: This is the word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning Elam at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah.
This is what the LORD of Hosts says: “Behold, I will shatter Elam’s bow, the mainstay of their might.
I will bring the four winds against Elam from the four corners of the heavens, and I will scatter them to all these winds. There will not be a nation to which Elam’s exiles will not go.

So I will shatter Elam before their foes, before those who seek their lives. I will bring disaster upon them, even My fierce anger,” declares the LORD. “I will send out the sword after them until I finish them off.
I will set My throne in Elam, and destroy its king and officials,” declares the LORD.
“Yet in the last days, I will restore Elam from captivity,” declares the LORD.

milcom.gloss: Milcom, the national god of the Ammonites, sometimes called Molech, associated elsewhere in Scripture with child sacrifice, 1 Kings 11:7. That Milcom goes into exile with his own priests, verse 3, shows him powerless to save the very people who served him.

shuvshevut.gloss: A Hebrew idiom meaning to turn or restore the captivity, that is, to reverse a nation's fortunes and bring its people home. It closes the oracles on Moab, 48:47, Ammon, 49:6, and Elam, 49:39, a small, recurring shadow of hope folded into even the harshest judgments.

basic.context: This chapter strings together five short oracles against Judah's remaining near neighbors: Ammon, who had seized Israelite territory in Gad; Edom, Israel's own kin through Esau, proud in her mountain strongholds; Damascus, the old Aramean capital; Kedar and Hazor, unwalled tent dwelling peoples of the eastern desert; and Elam, far to the east. Each is judged for its own particular offense, whether land grabbing, pride, or violence, yet three of the five, Ammon, Moab in the previous chapter, and Elam, close with a promise that the LORD will one day restore what He has broken.
basic.hermeneutics: These are real historical oracles against real ancient peoples, substantially fulfilled through the campaigns of Babylon and, in the case of Kedar and Hazor, explicitly tied to a Babylonian defeat, verse 28. They are not predictions about modern nations bearing similar names. The abiding truth is that the LORD's justice is not partial to Israel's enemies alone or to Israel's kin alone; He judges every nation by the same standard, and every nation, however judged, remains within reach of His mercy.
basic.originalLanguages: Milcom, Ammon's god, is named twice and shown powerless, exiled with his own priests, verse 3. Across three of these oracles the Hebrew idiom shuv shevut, to restore the captivity, appears as a settled formula of hope, verses 6 and 39, showing that even the LORD's severest sentences are not always His last word for a nation.
basic.typology: The recurring shuv shevut promise, restoration from captivity for humbled nations, anticipates the wider ingathering of the nations promised through Christ, in whom people from Ammon, Edom, and Elam's regions would one day be reconciled to God, Ephesians 2:11-13. Edom's proud eagle's nest brought down from the rocks, verse 16, anticipates every high thing that exalts itself against God being humbled before Christ, 2 Corinthians 10:5.
basic.christ: Across five different peoples, the LORD's justice and mercy hold together: judgment falls in full, yet Ammon and Elam are promised restoration, and Edom's orphans and widows are told, remarkably, 'I will preserve their lives, let your widows trust in Me,' verse 11, mercy spoken even into an oracle of near total destruction. This pattern, wrath poured out yet mercy still offered, is fulfilled at the cross, where Christ absorbed the full wrath the nations deserved so that from Ammon to Elam, from the ends of the earth, a people could be gathered into God's family, Acts 2:9 lists Elamites among those who heard the gospel at Pentecost.
basic.god: God is sovereign over every nation regardless of size, geography, or kinship to Israel: walled Damascus, unwalled Kedar, mountain bound Edom, and distant Elam all answer to the same LORD of Hosts. His anger against pride and violence is real and unsparing, yet His compassion reaches even further, holding out restoration to nations that, from a human point of view, had earned only destruction.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 19:36-38 and Genesis 25:1-4 trace Ammon and Moab's, and later Edom's, kinship to Israel through Lot and Esau. Obadiah gives an entire prophecy devoted to Edom's judgment for violence against Jacob. Acts 2:9 lists Elamites among the nations present at Pentecost, an early sign of the promised restoration reaching even that distant people. Ephesians 2:11-13 describes Gentiles once far off being brought near through Christ.
basic.oneStory: Five very different nations, near kin and distant strangers alike, are shown answering to the same LORD, and three of the five are promised restoration even after severe judgment. That widening circle of mercy toward the nations comes to its fullness in Christ, in whom people from Ammon to Elam, once far off, are brought near and gathered into the one family of God.

context.literary:
Jeremiah 49 is a gathering of five panels, each introduced by the same kind of heading, 'Concerning,' and each answering a different kind of nation. The order is not geographic and it is not chronological. It moves from a kinsman across the Jordan, Ammon, verses 1 to 6, to a kinsman to the south, Edom, verses 7 to 22, then to a city state to the north, Damascus, verses 23 to 27, then to desert nomads in the east, Kedar and Hazor, verses 28 to 33, and finally to the far highland kingdom of Elam, verses 34 to 39. The circle widens from brothers to strangers, and in the end it reaches the edge of the known world. The LORD's court has no outside.

The panels are unequal on purpose. Edom takes sixteen verses, because Edom was the closest relative and carried the heaviest charge, and Elam takes six. Within them the oracles lean on one another. The lion from the thickets of the Jordan, verses 19 to 21, returns word for word against Babylon at Jeremiah 50:44-46. The 'eagle' of verse 22 recalls the eagle of Moab in Jeremiah 48:40. The woman in labor, verses 22 and 24 here and Jeremiah 50:43 later, becomes the book's emblem for a warrior who has lost his nerve. Verses 14 to 16 on Edom are very close to Obadiah 1 to 4, and verses 9 and 10 to Obadiah 5 and 6, so Jeremiah and Obadiah share a source or one has used the other.

The frame is a pattern of promise. Ammon's oracle closes with 'Yet afterward I will restore the Ammonites from captivity,' verse 6, and Elam's with 'Yet in the last days, I will restore Elam from captivity,' verse 39. The two promises stand like bookends around the central three panels, which end in desolation. Edom has one very different hint of mercy, in the middle of its judgment, at verse 11, where the LORD says of the orphans of the doomed, 'I will preserve their lives.'
context.historical:
The five peoples did not share a map or a politics, but Jeremiah's hearers would have known them all. Ammon, descended from Lot, Genesis 19:38, held the territory east of the Jordan around Rabbah, today Amman. David's general Joab had fought at Rabbah, 2 Samuel 12:26-29, and the Ammonites had pushed into the Israelite land of Gad during the weakness of the northern tribes. Jeremiah 40:14 and 41:15 show Baalis king of Ammon sponsoring the plot that killed Gedaliah after Jerusalem fell. Ammon's god is Milcom, linked in 1 Kings 11:33 with Chemosh and with Ashtoreth in Solomon's idolatry.

Edom was Israel's blood relative. The nation grew from Esau, Genesis 36:8, and settled in Mount Seir, where Israel was told not to provoke them, Deuteronomy 2:4-5. Yet Edom refused Israel passage at the Exodus, Numbers 20:14-21, and Psalm 137:7 remembers Edom's cry 'tear it down to its foundations' when Jerusalem fell. The towns of Teman and Bozrah, and the rock fortresses of verse 16, belonged to a country of narrow gorges and heights that made invasion hard. Later, Edomites pressed into the south of Judah, and the region came to be called Idumea. It was an Idumean family that produced Herod the Great, and Mark 3:8 lists Idumea among the places from which crowds came to Jesus.

Damascus, the Aramean capital, was an old foe in the days of Ben-hadad and Hazael, which Amos 1:3-5 names. Kedar and Hazor are not the Hazor of Joshua but desert Arab peoples, and the oracle itself says Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon 'defeated' them, verse 28. A Babylonian chronicle, outside Scripture, records a raid on Arab tribes about the year 599 BC. Jeremiah 9:25-26 and 25:23 mention the desert peoples who 'clip the hair of their temples,' the habit the oracle names in verse 32. Elam lay east of Babylon in what is now southwest Iran. The oracle is dated to the opening of Zedekiah's reign, verse 34, around 597 BC, when the neighbours were weighing whether to follow Egypt in revolt, Jeremiah 27:3.
context.canonical:
These oracles are a small chapter in a large conversation. The cup of wrath that Jeremiah 49:12 places in Edom's hand is the cup of Jeremiah 25:15-17, which the prophet was told to make all nations drink, and Jeremiah 25:21 lists Edom, Moab and Ammon among the drinkers, with Elam named at 25:25. Lamentations 4:21 uses the same image, 'the cup will pass to you as well.' Edom's story is told again in Obadiah, in Isaiah 34:5-6, where the LORD's sword has a sacrifice in Bozrah, in Ezekiel 25:12-14 and 35, and in Malachi 1:2-4, where Edom's plan to rebuild is answered with the verdict that it will be a wasteland. Isaiah 63:1 sees a figure coming from Edom, from Bozrah, in crimson garments.

Ammon appears in Amos 1:13-15, which charges the Ammonites with cruelty to Gilead's pregnant women, and Zephaniah 2:8-11 pairs Ammon with Moab. Damascus is answered at Isaiah 17:1 and Amos 1:3-5. Kedar's glory is to vanish in Isaiah 21:16-17, yet Isaiah 60:7 and 42:11 bring Kedar into worship. Elam is among the places from which the LORD will recover the remnant of His people, Isaiah 11:11.

The New Testament takes the promised restoration seriously. Amos 9:11-12 foresees Israel possessing 'the remnant of Edom and all the nations that bear My name,' and James quotes it at Acts 15:16-17 to explain why Gentiles are welcomed without becoming Jews. Acts 2:9 lists Elamites in the Pentecost crowd. Ephesians 2:13 says those 'once far away have been brought near through the blood of Christ.' Paul quotes Malachi's 'Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated' at Romans 9:13, which shows that Edom's story has been taken into the argument about God's free choice.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
In the first years of Zedekiah, the small kingdoms around Judah were talking about rebellion against Babylon, and Jerusalem was tempted to listen. Jeremiah's task in this chapter is to show Judah that the nations she might join are already sentenced, and that their strengths are not strengths. Edom has height, Ammon has fertile valleys and money, Damascus has walls, Kedar has distance, and Elam has the bow. The oracle says each of these will fail under the same hand. Judah's best course is submission to Babylon for the time being, because the God who raised Babylon will also bring her down in His own time.

The chapter also teaches that the LORD's justice is specific. Ammon is charged with taking the land of Gad. Edom is charged with pride in her mountains, and with the cup that her own relatives had to drink and that she assumed she would escape. Damascus is charged with panic and with being a city of praise that is forsaken. Kedar is charged with false security, 'a nation at ease,' and Elam with trust in her bow. Where a promise of restoration appears, it is a deliberate hint that the God who judges has not stopped caring for any people.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is a record of what the LORD said about particular peoples in a particular generation. It is not a charter for hostility toward the descendants of these peoples. Edom, Ammon and Elam are not code names for any modern nation, and the oracles do not instruct believers to hate or to attack. The one command-like line, 'Abandon your orphans; I will preserve their lives,' verse 11, is addressed to the doomed and is a promise, not a rule.

The lasting pattern is that God judges pride, greed and security in strength, and that He extends mercy beyond what the offender expects. Believers can apply that to themselves, to their own fortresses and their own prosperity. They can also apply the pastoral side: the LORD is the defender of the fatherless and of widows, Psalm 68:5, even in the middle of a judgment on their nation. Obedience means leaving vengeance where Jeremiah leaves it, with the LORD.

debates.question: How is Edom's cup to be understood, 'if those who do not deserve to drink the cup must drink it, can you possibly remain unpunished?' verse 12?

views.label: Judah is the undeserving drinker
views.case: The 'innocent' who must drink are Judah and the people of the covenant, who are suffering at Babylon's hands. Lamentations 4:21 says the cup will pass to Edom as well. The argument is from lesser to greater: if Judah, who is at least in the LORD's house, drinks the cup, Edom cannot hope to escape it.

views.label: A general principle about the nations
views.case: The verse says no more than that if even those less deserving of judgment suffer, the guilty will not be spared. Jeremiah 25:28-29 says the same of any nation that tries to refuse the cup, and it argues that if God starts with His own city, He will not skip the rest.

debates.bearing: The two readings give the same conclusion. Edom is warned that exemption from a judgment that is falling on everyone is not possible. The text does not call Judah innocent. It only says Judah drinks first.

debates.question: What does it mean that Ammon, Elam and, in the previous chapter, Moab are promised restoration, but Edom, Damascus and Kedar are not?

views.label: A real difference in how the LORD treats each nation
views.case: Edom's oracle says 'ruins forever,' verse 13, and Hazor will be 'a desolation forever,' verse 33, while Ammon and Elam receive a promise. The simplest reading is that the text intends the contrast. Malachi 1:4 says of Edom that whatever it rebuilds, the LORD will tear down.

views.label: Restoration is for the nations as a whole, and the omission is incidental
views.case: The same LORD promises the nations a future, and a verse such as Amos 9:12 speaks of the remnant of Edom. The silence at Edom's end may only mean that the oracle stresses the permanence of the physical ruin, not that individuals and descendants are shut out of mercy. Verse 11 has an unexpected mercy even inside the oracle against Edom.

views.label: The language is to be read by the New Testament
views.case: Others say it is the gospel that settles who is included, and that Acts 15:16-17 reads Amos 9:11-12, with its Edom, as the future of the Gentiles generally.

debates.bearing: The text does not tell us why some oracles end in hope and others do not. The safest reading holds the contrast and the promise together: some places will stay desolate, and some people from every nation will be gathered. Verse 11 shows that mercy to the vulnerable is open even where the national verdict is final.

study.originalLanguages:
The basic level has named Milcom and the formula of restoring captivity. Several other turns of phrase in the chapter reward a closer look.

At verse 1 the Hebrew sets two words side by side that the English can hide. The Ammonites are said to have 'taken possession' of Gad, and Israel is asked 'Is he without heir?' The verb for taking possession and the word for an heir come from one root, which means to inherit or dispossess. Verse 2 turns it round: Israel will drive out 'their dispossessors,' again with the same family of words. The land swap is told in the vocabulary of inheritance, and the sting is that the Ammonites are behaving as heirs of what belongs to Israel's family. The BSB footnote at verse 1 notes that the name 'Milcom' can be read as 'their king,' so that the accusation has a second sense: 'why has their king taken possession of Gad?' The same ambiguity is in verse 3. The footnote adds that Milcom is a variant of Molech, and Leviticus 18:21 forbids giving children to Molech.

At verse 7 the question 'Is there no longer wisdom in Teman?' is a rhetorical sneer at Edom's old reputation. Teman was known for its sages. Obadiah 1:8-9 says the wise men of Edom will be destroyed. 'Wisdom' here is the quick shrewdness of a people who had always managed to survive. The next verses use trade images, a vintager who leaves gleanings and thieves who steal only what they want, verse 9, and then say the LORD will strip Esau bare. Obadiah 5 uses the same pair, so the image circulated among the prophets.

The 'clefts of the rocks' of verse 16 is the Hebrew picture of a people who live in hollows in the cliff. The BSB footnote notes the alternative 'of Sela,' the Hebrew word for rock, which is a place name. The eagle's nest, which is set high, is an image of the proud who feel unreachable. Verse 22 reuses the eagle against Bozrah, so the bird of security becomes the bird of attack. Between those two verses the lion rises 'from the thickets of the Jordan,' and the people are told it is the LORD's own choosing, 'Who is the chosen one I will appoint for this?' The verb means to commission, and the question is rhetorical: no one outranks the One who commissions.

At verse 25, 'the city of praise' and 'the town that brings Me joy' are tender phrases for Damascus. They may be the LORD's own regret, or they may be an ironic echo of how the city boasted of itself. Verse 29 gives the cry 'Terror is on every side!' This phrase, magor missabib, is Jeremiah's signature, found in Jeremiah 6:25, 20:3 and 20:10, where his own enemies turn it on him. When it appears here in the mouths of Kedar's raiders, it means the invaders will use the very formula Jeremiah was mocked for. The footnote at verse 33 gives 'serpents or dragons' as an alternative to 'jackals,' showing the same uncertainty as the Hebrew tannim at Jeremiah 51:37.

Last, Elam's 'bow' in verse 35 is called 'the mainstay of their might,' literally the first or chief of their strength. Isaiah 22:6 pictures Elam taking up the quiver. And in verse 38 the LORD says, 'I will set My throne in Elam.' The throne is the seat of the judge, and God here sits in the capital of a distant people, which is as clear a statement as the Old Testament has that His court reaches beyond its borders.

typology.type: The nations who are restored, Jeremiah 49:6 and 49:39
typology.fulfillment: The shuv shevut promises over Ammon and Elam are early signs of a mercy that spills outside Israel. Acts 2:9 includes Elamites among the Pentecost crowd who hear the wonders of God in their own languages, and Ephesians 2:13 says those 'who once were far away have been brought near through the blood of Christ.' The correspondence is that nations judged are also nations promised. The type falls short because the Old Testament promise says only that the LORD will restore them from captivity, and the New Testament shows the full measure, a place in one family without being first made Israel.

In the middle of a verdict, the LORD says 'Abandon your orphans; I will preserve their lives. Let your widows trust in Me.' It is the character of the God who is 'a father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows,' Psalm 68:5. Christ embodies it. He says 'I will not leave you as orphans,' John 14:18, and James 1:27 names the care of orphans and widows as pure religion. The type falls short because Jeremiah speaks to survivors in a single nation, and Christ speaks to every person who is bereft.

typology.type: The one who comes from Edom, Isaiah 63:1
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah 49 is not about a Messiah, but the closest neighbour text, Isaiah 63:1, sees a figure coming from Edom and Bozrah, 'mighty to save,' with garments stained crimson. The New Testament uses the image of the garment dipped in blood for the returning Christ, Revelation 19:13. The correspondence is that the LORD Himself takes up the judgment on Edom and carries it to the end. The type is partial because Isaiah's stained garments are the result of treading the winepress, while Revelation adds that the blood is also His own, Revelation 5:9.

study.christ:
This chapter does not mention a king from David's line or a servant, and it would be wrong to force a Messiah into every oracle. It leads to Christ by what it shows about the world He enters, and by three small seams in the poetry.

The first seam is the cup. In Jeremiah 49:12 the LORD asks whether the one who does not deserve to drink the cup can possibly escape it. In Jeremiah 25:15-17 the cup is the wine of wrath, and the nations stagger and go out of their minds. In Gethsemane Jesus prays 'My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me,' Matthew 26:39, and in John 18:11 He says 'Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?' The one who did not deserve to drink drank it. That is the answer to the question of verse 12 which the chapter itself could not give. Judgment on the nations is real, and it is carried by Christ for those who come to Him.

The second seam is the promise of restoration at the beginning and the end of the chapter. 'Yet afterward I will restore the Ammonites from captivity,' verse 6, and 'in the last days, I will restore Elam,' verse 39. These are not a promise of national comebacks alone. The phrase 'the last days' is the vocabulary the prophets use for the age of the Messiah. Acts 2:9 records Elamites at Pentecost, and Ephesians 2:13 says that people from far away have been brought near through His blood. The wall that kept nations out has been broken, Ephesians 2:14.

The third seam is the mercy to the vulnerable in verse 11. In an oracle of near total ruin, the LORD says 'Let your widows trust in Me.' That is the God who will say through His Son that He cares for the little ones and who gives Himself as the defender of those with no one else. Jesus teaches that what is done to the least is done to Him, Matthew 25:40.

The chapter also leads to Christ by contrast. Edom hid in the clefts of the rock and raised her nest like an eagle's, verse 16. The Son came down. He had no nest, as He says in Matthew 8:20, and Philippians 2:6-8 tells how He emptied Himself. Edom's pride in her strength is answered by the weakness in which He saves.

A caution is in order. Edom, Damascus, Kedar and Elam are not secretly pictures of Christ, and the lion of verse 19 is the LORD Himself, not the Messiah in disguise. The links above rest on the New Testament's own reading of the cup, the nations and the orphans. The oracle gives the problem and a hope, and Christ is the one in whom the hope is kept.
study.god:
What the chapter shows about God is first of all that His government has no frontier. In five panels He addresses a kinsman across the Jordan, a kinsman to the south, a city of the north, desert tent-dwellers and a distant highland kingdom. He tells Elam 'I will set My throne in Elam,' verse 38. A tribal deity ruled his own territory. The LORD rules every territory, and Jeremiah puts Him on the throne of a land that never worshipped Him.

Second, His judgments answer particular charges. He asks why Milcom has taken possession of Gad, verse 1. He tells Edom that the terror she causes and the pride of her heart have deceived her, verse 16. He tells Kedar that it is 'a nation at ease,' verse 31, and tells Elam that its bow is the mainstay of its might, verse 35. In every case the nation's security has been its idol. The God who judges is the God who sees what each people trusts, and who knows the difference between what they say and what they are.

Third, He is sworn to His word. 'By Myself I have sworn,' verse 13, is the strongest form of a promise or a threat in Scripture, and Hebrews 6:13 says that when God had no one greater to swear by, He swore by Himself. The oath is not decoration. It shows that God's verdict on Edom is as certain as His promise to Abraham.

Fourth, He is incomparable. The lion passage, verse 19, ends with three questions: 'Who is like Me, and who can challenge Me? What shepherd can stand against Me?' The word 'shepherd' is the common title for a king, so the question is who among the kings of the earth can face Him. The same sentence recurs word for word against Babylon at Jeremiah 50:44, which makes the point that He is not committed to any empire.

Fifth, He does not forget the weak. In the middle of the verdict on Edom He says, 'Abandon your orphans; I will preserve their lives,' verse 11. The LORD who disarms a nation does not lose track of its widows. Psalm 68:5 names Him the father of the fatherless.

And sixth, He keeps back mercy as well as wrath. Ammon and Elam receive a promise in the same breath as a sentence. It is not that the sentence is softened but that the God who passes it has more to say.

For worship, the chapter calls believers to reverence for a God no nation can hide from, to humility about any wall or fortune they trust, and to a hope that does not exclude the stranger. Revelation 15:4 says 'All nations will come and worship before You,' and Jeremiah 49 is one of the places that prepared for that sentence.

crossReferences.note: Obadiah's vision against Edom shares much of Jeremiah 49:9 and 14 to 16: the envoy sent to the nations, the pride of dwellers in the clefts of the rock, the eagle's nest, and the thieves who leave gleanings. Reading the two together shows how the prophets handed on one verdict, and Obadiah adds the reason, Edom's violence against Jacob.

The prophet is told to take the cup of the wine of wrath and make all the nations drink. Jeremiah 49:12 shows the cup arriving at Edom's door. The two passages make the oracles of chapters 46 to 51 a single act, with each nation taking its turn.

Edom is told she may rejoice for now, but the cup will pass to her too and expose her sins. It is the grieving side of Jeremiah 49:12, and it shows that Edom's gloating over Jerusalem's fall was a major part of the charge.

Amos accuses Ammon of ripping open the pregnant women of Gilead to enlarge their territory, and promises fire on the walls of Rabbah. It gives the deeds behind Jeremiah's brief question about who took possession of Gad.

Amos threatens the house of Hazael and the citadels of Ben-hadad. Jeremiah 49:27 uses the same name for Damascus, 'the fortresses of Ben-hadad,' showing a settled prophetic tradition against the Aramean capital.

All the glory of Kedar will be gone within a year, and the remaining archers will be few. Jeremiah 49:28-33 is the Babylonian fulfilment of this kind of sentence, and the two prophets agree on the end of Kedar's power.

After the exile, Edom says 'we will rebuild the ruins,' and the LORD answers that He will tear down what they build. It shows how Jeremiah's 'ruins forever' in 49:13 was understood by the later community.

Hebrews says that God, having no one greater, swore by Himself to Abraham. Jeremiah 49:13 uses the same oath against Edom, 'by Myself I have sworn.' The oath that secures the promise to Abraham also secures the verdict on Bozrah.

The fallen tent of David will be rebuilt so that his people may possess 'the remnant of Edom and all the nations that bear My name.' Edom is named among those to be gathered, which colors how the severity of Jeremiah 49 is to be taken.

James quotes Amos 9:11-12 to explain why Gentiles are welcome in the church without being circumcised. The restored tent of David includes the nations, and the promise held in oracles like Jeremiah 49:6 and 49:39 is opened to them.

Elamites are named among the crowd at Pentecost who hear the wonders of God in their own languages. This is the moment where a people once judged in Jeremiah 49:34-39 hear the gospel, and it is the nearest New Testament echo of the promise to restore Elam.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's first nations are named in Genesis 10, and the next chapter shows them scattered at Babel. The peoples of this chapter are among their heirs: Elam is a son of Shem, Genesis 10:22, Ammon is born of Lot's younger daughter, Genesis 19:38, and Edom is Esau, who sold a birthright and settled in Seir, Genesis 25:30 and 36:8. The promise that the older will serve the younger, Genesis 25:23, runs under the whole history of Edom and Israel, and Malachi 1:2-3 and Romans 9:13 take it into the doctrine of God's choice.

The chapter answers the question that the story of the nations raises: what does God do about the peoples who surround His people and trust in their own strength? His answer is judgment on pride, whether the pride of a mountain stronghold or a fertile valley or a bow. The line from Genesis 3, where the serpent promised that humans would be like God, runs through each nation that says 'Who can come against me?' verse 4. The same story runs through Babel's tower and Babylon's empire, and Jeremiah 49 puts it in five short scenes.

Yet the story is not simply a catalogue of ruin. It carries forward the promise to Abraham that all the families of the earth will be blessed, Genesis 12:3. Ammon and Elam receive a restoration, Edom's orphans receive a promise, and Amos 9:11-12 sees the remnant of Edom possessed alongside all the nations that bear the LORD's name. Acts 15:16-17 reads that promise as fulfilled in the Gentile mission, and Acts 2:9 records Elamites at Pentecost.

At the cross the cup that Jeremiah 25 poured out for the nations is drunk by the Son, Matthew 26:39 and John 18:11, and the wall between near and far is broken, Ephesians 2:13-14. The story ends in the new creation, where the nations come and worship, Revelation 15:4, and where the kings of the earth bring their glory into the city, Revelation 21:24. The throne that the LORD set in Elam in Jeremiah 49:38 is the throne that Revelation 22:3 describes in the city where 'the throne of God and of the Lamb will be within the city,' and from which the curse is gone.

quiz.q: Why is Ammon indicted in verse 1?

options.text: Because her god Milcom had taken possession of Gad, Israelite territory.
options.note: Verse 1 opens with exactly this charge, Ammon's seizure of Israel's land.

options.text: Because Ammon had refused to pay tribute to Babylon.
options.note: Not the charge given in this text; the indictment concerns Ammon's seizure of Gad.

options.text: Because Ammon had allied with Egypt against Judah.
options.note: Plausible in general terms of ancient politics, but this specific oracle names the seizure of Gad as the offense.

options.text: Because Ammon had never worshiped any god.
options.note: The opposite; Ammon's worship of Milcom is explicitly named throughout the passage.

quiz.q: What is Edom's core sin according to verse 16?

options.text: The terror she caused and the pride of her heart, trusting her mountain strongholds.
options.note: Verse 16 names this pride and false security directly, comparing Edom to an eagle nesting among the rocks.

options.text: Refusing to worship any god at all.
options.note: Not the charge in this passage; Edom's sin named here is pride and false security, not irreligion.

options.text: Failing to pay taxes to Judah.
options.note: No such charge appears in this text.

options.text: Building too many cities.
options.note: Not quite; the issue is not the number of cities but the pride and false security they gave Edom.

quiz.q: What distinguishes Kedar and Hazor from the other nations judged in this chapter, according to verse 31?

options.text: They have no gates or bars and live alone, an unwalled and undefended people.
options.note: Verse 31 specifically describes this vulnerability, unlike the walled cities of Damascus or Edom's mountain strongholds.

options.text: They are the wealthiest of all the nations named.
options.note: Their wealth in camels and herds is mentioned, verse 32, but their defining feature named in verse 31 is their lack of walls.

options.text: They alone worship the LORD.
options.note: No such claim is made about Kedar and Hazor in this text.

options.text: They alone are spared from judgment.
options.note: Not so; Kedar and Hazor are judged severely in this passage, becoming a haunt for jackals, verse 33.

quiz.q: What promise closes the oracle against Elam, verse 39?

options.text: The LORD will restore Elam from captivity in the last days.
options.note: Verse 39 explicitly promises this restoration after Elam's severe judgment.

options.text: Elam will conquer Babylon and rule the region.
options.note: No such promise appears; the hope offered is restoration, not conquest.

options.text: Elam will be destroyed forever with no future mentioned.
options.note: The opposite; verse 39 explicitly promises future restoration.

options.text: Elam's king will be spared from judgment.
options.note: Not accurate; verse 38 explicitly says the LORD will destroy Elam's king and officials before the restoration promise in verse 39.

quiz.q: What unites the mercy shown to Ammon, Edom, and Elam in this chapter?

options.text: Each nation, though severely judged, is given some word of preserved life or future restoration.
options.note: Ammon and Elam receive the shuv shevut restoration formula, and Edom is told the LORD will preserve her orphans and widows, verse 11.

options.text: None of the three nations actually experiences any real judgment.
options.note: The opposite; all three undergo severe, real judgment in this chapter.

options.text: All three nations are promised they will replace Israel as God's people.
options.note: No such promise appears anywhere in this passage.

options.text: All three are promised exemption from the coming Babylonian invasion.
options.note: Not accurate; Babylon's invasion falls on all of them, but mercy is promised for a time after that judgment.

questions: Ammon boasted, 'Who can come against me?' trusting her fruitful valleys and riches. What resources or successes tempt you toward that same false security?
Edom trusted the height and inaccessibility of her mountain home, yet the LORD said, 'even from there I will bring you down.' What high place of self-sufficiency do you need to let God reach?
Even to Edom, under judgment, the LORD said, 'let your widows trust in Me.' Where in your own hardship is God inviting you to trust Him rather than despair?
Ammon and Elam are both promised restoration after judgment; God's mercy reaches even the nations most opposed to His people. Who in your life have you written off as beyond God's reach?

Elamites were present at Pentecost, hearing the gospel in their own language, a small fulfillment of the restoration promised here. How does it encourage you that God's plan for the nations he judges spans centuries, right into the New Testament?
